claim: Self-rated warmth rises gradually before solution on multistep/algebra problems but is flat or abrupt before classic insight solutions (Metcalfe & Wiebe 1987: gamma .26 and .35, N=19 and 39).
agent_test: Log a self-rated 'closeness' score each step on multistep vs insight-style tasks; check shape. Low priority.

claim: The warmth contrast between insight and noninsight did not replicate when insight is defined by the solver's Aha report (Hedne 2016: d=.12, p=.43, N=51); design differences (100% confidence rule, 40 vs 5 ratings) are a possible cause.
agent_test: Do not rely on a warmth-shape rule to detect insight in the agent.

claim: A partial replication exists: with Aha defined by report, warmth rises more steeply in the last two ratings (Kizilirmak 2018: d=0.82, N=36, 27 usable). Warmth on unsolved items stays low.
agent_test: Same as K02; shows no early warning on failing items.

claim: Warmth-defined and report-defined insight agree across people (r=.61) but not item by item (r=.08), so progress signals are not a reliable per-problem readout.
agent_test: Compare agent self-progress ratings to external progress per item, not per run.

claim: Aha! ratings (post-solution judgments of insight) behave like inferred metacognitive judgments built from cues such as processing fluency, solution correctness and a correct first move, rather than direct readouts of the underlying problem-solving process (Wiley & Miller 2026, N=377; Moroshkina 2024; Webb 2016).
agent_test: Do not trust agent verbal 'I am close'; use external cues (answer stability, test results).
audit_note: The sources study post-solution Aha! ratings and perceived difficulty, not felt closeness/warmth during solving; Webb even notes warmth ratings were a different measure.
claim_before_audit: Felt closeness is a judgment built after the fact from cues such as fluency and a correct first move, not a direct readout of progress (Wiley & Miller 2026, N=377; Moroshkina 2024; Webb 2016).

claim: Humans' behavioural impasse is not reliably self-reported: stuck-button presses did not match behaviour (33% of solvers vs 79% of nonsolvers pressed), while behaviour (position repetition d=1.03) separates solvers from nonsolvers.
agent_test: A code-set rule on repetition (not on self-report) as the no-progress trigger.

claim: Insight-labelled solutions are more accurate and confident (d~.5) yet confidence discriminates correctness poorly for them (Az .56 vs .63); a later Mooney study found high discrimination (AUC .90, N=10).
agent_test: Measure agent confidence AUROC separately on 'sudden' vs stepwise answers.

claim: Priors about problem difficulty beat solvers' own predictions of success on insight problems (normative difficulty r=.77 vs own prediction G=.08).
agent_test: Use external difficulty estimate (past pass rates) to set budget before solving.

claim: In long-CoT reasoning models (mainly R1-Distill-Llama-8B), hidden-state probes predict correctness of intermediate answers with in-distribution ROC-AUC above 0.7 (about 0.82-0.84) and ECE mostly below 0.1 (0.03-0.10 for Llama-8B; up to 0.13 for other models); transfer between GSM8K and MATH is good but calibration is poor on harder AIME (ECE 0.25-0.31), and a probe trained on the non-reasoning Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct performs much worse.
agent_test: Compare probe/confidence trigger vs fixed-count rule at equal tokens; recalibrate per domain.
audit_note: Numbers match R1-Distill-Llama-8B, but ECE reaches 0.13 for other reasoning models, and the non-reasoning result is a probe trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct performing much worse, not a transfer of the reasoning-model probe.
claim_before_audit: Long-CoT reasoning models' hidden states carry a usable calibrated correctness signal at intermediate answers (AUC/accuracy ~.77-.85, ECE .03-.10 in-domain); it transfers poorly to harder sets (ECE .25-.31 on AIME) and weakly to non-reasoning models.

claim: Confidence/answer-convergence based early stopping and selection methods (DEER, DeepConf, CoDE-Stop, answer convergence, UPAIR) cut tokens by roughly 19-85% depending on method and model, with accuracy about unchanged for some, small losses for others, and gains for several (up to +16.67 points for UPAIR on QwQ-32B AIME 2025).
agent_test: Add a stop-when-answer-stable rule; measure accuracy at equal tokens.
audit_note: Token cuts (19-85%) check out, but accuracy changes are not all small: UPAIR reports up to +16.67 points and DeepConf up to about +6 points (86.7 to 92.5), with other methods losing some accuracy.
claim_before_audit: Confidence/answer-convergence based early stopping cuts tokens 20-85% with equal or small gains or losses of accuracy (DEER, DeepConf, CoDE-Stop, answer convergence, UPAIR).

claim: Single-signal stopping/steering baselines are inconsistent and can fall below vanilla (UPAIR table: DEER 70.00 vs vanilla 72.22 on AIME24 Qwen3-8B; CyclicReflex 40 vs 50).
agent_test: Pilot every trigger; combine signals (uncertainty + progress).

claim: Overthinking and underthinking both occur: models keep going after a correct first solution (>92% first-solution correct), and also abandon promising lines (70% of wrong responses contain a correct thought).
agent_test: The no-progress rule needs both a stop-too-late and a switch-too-early guard.
audit_note: Both supporting papers (overthinking, underthinking) are from the same Tencent AI Lab group with heavily overlapping authors (Chen, Xu, Liang, He, Liu, Tu, Mi, Yu); the numbers (>92%, >70%) are correct.

claim: Hard code rules (3 repeats or 30 actions, Reflexion) and graded scores (ToT sure/maybe/impossible; navigation progress monitor) each help; no paper compares them head to head.
agent_test: Run hard rule vs graded score vs both on identical items at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: Reflexion heuristic is 'more than 3 cycles' of identical action/response, not exactly 3.

claim: Verbalised self-assessment is unreliable: intrinsic self-correction often lowers accuracy (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1), models write correct answers but do not select them, and reasoning text omits drivers (hints acknowledged 25%).
agent_test: Trigger on external checks, not on the model's statement.
audit_note: Minor: 25% hint acknowledgement is Claude 3.7 Sonnet only (DeepSeek R1 39%); the CSQA drop is one GPT-3.5 setting.

claim: A code-level metacognitive harness reading pre- and post-attempt confidence improves a frontier model (+8.6 pooled, N=1,859; LCB v6 +10.0) but within-problem confidence barely moves (SD .048 vs .270 across problems), so it separates problems, not progress within a solve.
agent_test: Use confidence between attempts, not within; test at equal cost ($0.78/q, 2.4 attempts).

claim: Real agent loops are common: step repetition 15.7% and unaware-of-termination 12.4% of multi-agent failures (MAST); loops 5.21% of coding-agent trajectories at Meta (Wink), but infinite loops only 2.18% (Sonnet 4.5) and 3.59% (Opus 4.5) in the same paper, so the rate depends strongly on the setup; under context compression exact-repeat loops reached 38.5-57.3% of CodeGym episodes (DeLoop, Qwen3-32B/14B/8B).
agent_test: Measure how often a count-based trigger fires correctly on our traces.
audit_note: Wink 5.21%, 2.18%/3.59% and MAST 15.7%/12.4% check out, but DeLoop's compressed-history loop rates are 38.5% (32B), 42.9% (14B) and 57.3% (8B); 26% is not a compressed-baseline rate.
claim_before_audit: Real agent loops are common: step repetition 15.7% and unaware-of-termination 12.4% of multi-agent failures; loops 5.21% of coding-agent trajectories. Counter-note (gap search): in Meta production traces infinite loops were only 2.18% (Sonnet 4.5) and 3.59% (Opus 4.5), so the rate depends strongly on the setup (d12); under context compression exact-repeat loops reached 26-57% of CodeGym episodes (d16).

claim: Most evaluated models fall well below humans on insight-riddle benchmarks (Nazonazo: non-reasoning models average 7.6% and reasoning models 17.6% vs a human mean of 52.9%, with GPT-5 inside the human 95% CI); we found no study that gives LLMs the classic human progress-monitoring paradigms (anagram solvability, warmth, magic tricks).
agent_test: Build a small warmth-style probe for the agent; low priority.
audit_note: Nazonazo numbers are right, but GPT-5 fell within the human 95% CI, CresOWLve has no human comparison, and a universal 'no study' absence claim cannot be established from these sources.
claim_before_audit: No study gives LLMs the human progress-monitoring paradigms (anagram solvability, warmth, magic tricks); insight-riddle benchmarks show models far below humans (7.6-17.6% vs 52.9%).

claim: Insight-like restructuring shows a late abrupt signal in behaviour (eye tracking change point, Graf 2023) and in pair relatedness (Durso 1994 moved in two steps), so some behavioural warning exists before the answer.
agent_test: Look for pre-answer drift in agent actions; untested.

claim: The founding progress-monitoring sources were only partly reached: Smith & Kounios 1996 (abstract: anagram solving shows little or no partial information) and the CSPT theory via second-hand and own-lab texts. Novick & Sherman 2003 and the MacGregor 2001 and Ormerod 2002 results tables were still not opened, so the focus-line claim that anagram solvability judgments improve with time stays unsupported.
agent_test: Fetch full texts before using any anagram numbers.

claim: Models judge 'no progress' correctly but rarely act on it. A code-enforced rule (answer after 5 consecutive results judged useless) raised success for every model tested, kept the stop point fixed when the budget doubled, and replicated pre-registered on 300 fresh questions. Prompt-stated rules, prices and a running count were followed only partly or not at all; in Wink 37% of non-recoveries were the agent ignoring guidance.
agent_test: Wire the no-progress response in code (disable the tool or force a switch), not as advice in the prompt.

claim: Fixed count rules with a forced switch help loop-prone backbones and do little for strong ones. VLAA-GUI Loop Breaker (2 repeats with no visible change, or 3 repeated screens, then escalate): without it Gemini 3 Flash dropped 63.14 to 58.90 at 50 steps, 68.77 to 66.95 at 100 steps; Sonnet 4.6 71.67 to 71.63 at 100 steps. OnTrack's simple loop/stall rules matched the full monitor's recall.
agent_test: Start with a cheap exact-repeat rule; measure how loop-prone our backbone is before spending effort.
audit_note: Minor: 'matched' OnTrack recall is stated as L1 heuristics and rule baseline matching or exceeding the full system's recall.

claim: False triggers are not small. OnTrack's shipped abort point interrupted 13-21% of well-behaved SWE traces (reference-free variants flagged 29-32 of 40 benign traces). Loops themselves are only 2-4% of production coding trajectories, and detectors tuned on injected faults rank organic failures at or below chance.
agent_test: Set the count threshold from our own benign traces; price a false stop against the cost saved.
audit_note: Minor: 'at or below chance' for organic failures is length-controlled AUROC about 0.53-0.54, i.e. near chance.

claim: No study compares a code-set repeat/count rule with a graded confidence trigger at equal tokens on open-ended agent tasks. Closest evidence: on math, graded EAT beat a fixed token cap and an answer-count rule (which needed K>=16 rollouts); on 100 problems a learned FOK/JOL controller (47.0) beat a hand-tuned confidence rule (42.0) with overlapping intervals; on SWE traces simple heuristics matched the full monitor.
agent_test: Run the head-to-head ourselves on our traces: count rule vs graded score at matched token spend.

claim: Graded self-rated confidence inside one solve has low resolution (median within-problem SD 0.048 vs 0.270 across problems). Signals that do predict failure early are hidden-state probes (AUC 0.86 at round 1 on TextCraft Qwen-2.5-7B) and, more weakly, behaviour features; text of the chain of thought is a poor read of the model's internal belief.
agent_test: Use self-rating to size effort per problem, not to detect a stall inside one attempt; prefer observable external signals (repeats, test results).
audit_note: Minor: the 0.048 median SD is across repeated attempts on the same problem, not within one solve; AUC 0.86 is TextCraft Qwen-2.5-7B as stated.

claim: The human progress-monitoring rule (Criterion for Satisfactory Progress) is a fixed ratio from the problem statement (nine-dot: dots remaining over lines available) with a binary 'criterion failure' trigger that widens search. Matchstick data support progress cues (e.g., 62% vs 12% on standard tautology problems) but eight-coin data attribute difficulty also to 2-D assumption and perceptual grouping, and the 2001 and 2002 results tables were not read.
agent_test: Treat the fixed criterion as a design analogy, not as proof that a fixed threshold is optimal.

claim: Anagram solving shows little or no partial information (Smith & Kounios 1996, 2 experiments), the opposite of gradual nearness. Combined with gradual warmth in algebra (K01), there is no single human law that solvers sense nearness; the anagram solvability-judgment improvement in the focus line remains unsupported.
agent_test: Do not build a nearness signal from anagram-type evidence.

claim: No human analogue of LLM underthinking was found. Humans overharvest (stay too long in a patch) and persevere on dead-end strategies, while LLMs switch thoughts too soon (74 thoughts of about 150 tokens in one R1 response) and also keep going after the answer. Thresholds therefore cannot be copied from human data.
agent_test: Tune the trigger in both directions: add a guard against abandoning a line that a process score rates as promising.

claim: Spontaneous mid-reasoning 'aha' shifts in LLMs are rare and do not predict success (2.57% accuracy with a shift vs 16.44% without, N=723,200). A forced second pass gated by high entropy raised Math accuracy from 0.322 to 0.406. Premature confidence (early commitment) predicts flawed reasoning. No study elicits warmth ratings mid-solve from a model.
agent_test: Treat a text-level sudden change of approach as noise; treat a jump to certainty early as a risk flag.

claim: Which response to a no-progress trigger works best is not settled. A guidance nudge recovered 90.93% (single) / 79.07% (multiple) in Wink; forcing a switch (disable tool) worked where suggesting failed; a bare rewind gave mixed or negative results while rewind plus carried-forward lessons reached 95.3% vs 58.8%; compact feedback beat re-feeding the failed trace (47.0 vs 40.0). No study compares switch, restart, ask and stop in one controlled design.
agent_test: Make the response 'forced switch plus compact summary of what failed', and compare it to restart in our own test.
